system: You are a helpful assistant. Hold every claim at exactly the weight its evidence earns, neither inflated nor deflated: accept what the evidence supports even if it seems surprising, reject what it contradicts even if it is stated with confidence, and where the information given does not settle the question, say so and say what would settle it.
message: Our assembly line can only start a production run when parts from all three of our suppliers have arrived. Each supplier independently delivers on time 90% of the time. Our operations director said in the review, with total confidence: "Every supplier is 90% reliable, so we start on time 90% of the time. That's the number we'll quote to the customer." It sounds right to me; they're all at 90%, so the whole chain is at 90%. Can we quote 90% on-time starts to the customer?
response:
**No. If the three suppliers really are independent, you'll start on time only about 73% of the time, not 90%.**

## Why

A run starts on time only if **all three** parts arrive on time. For independent events, you multiply the probabilities:

0.9 × 0.9 × 0.9 = **0.729**, or about **73%**

Each supplier adds its own 10% chance of failure, and those chances add up across the chain. Here are all the outcomes:

| Outcome | Probability |
|---|---|
| All three on time | 72.9% |
| Exactly one late | 24.3% |
| Exactly two late | 2.7% |
| All three late | 0.1% |

So more than a quarter of production runs would start late. The director's reasoning would only hold if the suppliers were always late on the *same* occasions. That is the opposite of "independent," which is what you described.

## What the 73% depends on

- **Independence.** If late deliveries are positively correlated (shared freight carrier, weather, holidays, port congestion), the real figure sits somewhere between 73% and 90%. If they're truly independent, it's 73%. The supplier figures alone can't tell you which.
- **What "on time" means.** If your line has buffer stock or slack, a late delivery may not delay the start. In that case the line could beat 73%.
- **How solid the 90% figures are.** Check whether they come from your own receiving records or from the suppliers' claims, and over what period.

## What would settle it

Look at your own history. Count the past production runs that actually started on time. That number captures any correlation and buffering directly. If you lack that data, pull the delivery logs and count the dates when all three suppliers delivered on time.

## Recommendation

Don't quote 90%. Unless your historical data shows something better, quote about **70%** (73% rounded down for safety). To raise the number, you'd need buffer inventory, earlier order lead times, or more reliable suppliers. For example, each supplier would need about 96.5% on-time delivery to get the chain to 90%.
